Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette:
Jabari was seven years old when he watched his father beat his mother in their living room. He remembers it not as a story but as a series of snapshots: the sharp crack of the first slap, his mother’s eyes widening in disbelief, the way his father’s silhouette loomed against the window. He stood frozen in the doorway, his body locked in a posture he would later recognize as the same one that returned in moments of sudden touch or silence. He couldn’t move, couldn’t call out, and afterward he told himself he should have done something—a thought that burrowed into him and stayed.

That feeling of helplessness shaped the years that followed. He began avoiding places he didn’t know, because he couldn’t assess the danger there. Silence made his stomach tighten; he felt sure something bad was about to happen. He started noticing objects that could be used as weapons—a beer bottle on a table, a screwdriver left on a counter—and scanning for them before anything else. That constant sense of imminent danger kept the memory coiled just beneath the surface; on nights when his hypervigilance was at its highest, the image of his father’s silhouette would surface unbidden, as if the threat itself had summoned it. Feeling this threatened all the time, he had quietly concluded that he must be permanently damaged—that the fear itself was proof he wasn't the person he used to be. His mother eventually left his father, but for Jabari the threat never really left.

At eighteen, he became a police officer—a job that, he thought, would let him be the one who acted instead of the one who froze. Instead, it put him directly in the path of his triggers every day. Patrolling a quiet residential block at dusk, the unusual silence would press against his ears, and the snapshot memory of that living room would flash: his mother’s face, his father’s arm. After that image surfaced, even the most ordinary things—the hum of a refrigerator, a door slamming in the station—felt like warnings he couldn't afford to ignore. That memory, in turn, made him scan more intently for weapons, confirming his sense that danger was near. He came to believe that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy—a thought that made every minor discomfort, a person acting suspiciously or an unexpected touch on the shoulder, feel like a warning signal of imminent collapse. That belief—that he was losing his grip on reality—meant that even neutral situations could become triggers, because his own mind had become the most convincing sign that something was wrong. That belief—that he was losing his grip on reality—kept pulling him back to the image of himself frozen in the doorway, as if the memory itself could confirm that he truly was falling apart.

One afternoon, a colleague clapped him on the back in a briefing room. Jabari’s body instantly locked—the same frozen posture from when he was seven—and the snapshot of his mother’s eyes returned with a wave of grief so sharp he had to excuse himself. The memory reinforced his belief that he couldn’t rely on himself; if a friendly pat could incapacitate him, how could he handle a real threat? That self-doubt drove him to check every corner, every shadow, every unfamiliar street, and the more he checked, the more he noticed potential weapons and suspicious movements, which triggered new memories and deepened his sense that he was losing control.

The cycle tightened over weeks. His hypervigilance turned ordinary interactions into triggers: a shopper acting oddly made him replay the moment his father’s hand connected; the hush in an elevator brought back the silence before the first blow. Each trigger revived the memory, and each memory strengthened his helplessness. He began avoiding unfamiliar parts of his beat, asking for reassignment to the same two blocks he knew, but even there he couldn’t shake the feeling that he was about to be caught off guard.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night when he pulled over a car for a minor infraction. The driver’s sudden movement toward the glove box made Jabari’s mind go blank—he later realized he had frozen, just like when he was seven, while his hand rested inches from his service weapon. He drove home shaking, certain he was going crazy, unable to trust himself on duty. In the clinic, he said he wasn’t sure what he was most afraid of: that he would freeze again, or that he would finally stop caring and react the wrong way. Either way, he wanted the snapshots to stop. "After that image surfaced, even ordinary sounds—a car backfiring, a raised voice on the radio—felt like warnings that the past was about to repeat itself."

What finally brought him to seek help was a night when he pulled over a car for a minor infraction. The driver’s sudden movement toward the glove box made Jabari’s mind go blank—he later realized he had frozen, just like when he was seven, while his hand rested inches from his service weapon. He drove home shaking, certain he was going crazy, unable to trust himself on duty. In the clinic, he said he wasn’t sure what he was most afraid of: that he would freeze again, or that he would finally stop caring and react the wrong way. Either way, he wanted the snapshots to stop. "After that image surfaced, even ordinary sounds—a car backfiring, a raised voice on the radio—felt like warnings that the past was about to repeat itself."
